title: AI push is putting banks at mercy of tech firms, warns Moody's
content:
The rating agency Moody’s has said the race to adopt AI is putting big banks at the mercy of a small group of Silicon Valley firms, leaving them vulnerable to widespread outages and price gouging by profit-hungry tech bosses.
The financial sector’s efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues across the City and Wall Street, Moody’s said.
But that will require “substantial investments”, and with so many rivals racing towards the same goal, many of those benefits will end up being “competed away”.
AI will also create bigger risks around data privacy, cybersecurity, fraud and so-called “deposit flight”, as well as an overdependence on a small number of tech firms, the rating agency warned.
That will raise concerns for bosses across the financial sector. More than 75% of City companies now use AI, according to a UK Treasury select committee report published in January, with insurers and international banks among the biggest adopters. They are mostly using it to automate administrative tasks or even help with core operations, including processing insurance claims and assessing customers’ creditworthiness.
“The reliance of most financial firms on a relatively small set of foundation AI model and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency,” the Moody’s report said.
“This is because a model outage at one major provider could potentially spread quickly across customers and sectors. As AI adoption deepens, regulators may increase their focus on operational resilience and third-party concentration in the AI model stack.”
The AI race also risked creating “vendor dependence risk”, Moody’s said, meaning that “a set of dominant AI model and infrastructure providers could, over time, exert control over the price of AI services”. That issue is likely to emerge as the bosses of loss-making generative AI companies, including the ChatGPT creator OpenAI and the Claude owner Anthropic, come under pressure to deliver profits for investors.
“While this could pose credit risks to financial firms, they would nevertheless retain control over key assets, including proprietary data,” Moody’s said. Many big banks and insurers also have longstanding experience negotiating down tech contracts, and may be using open-source AI models, and striking key partnerships, to try to offset “dependency risks”.
Lloyds Banking Group’s chief executive, Charlie Nunn, recently doubled down on AI investment plans with a £13bn strategy that would involve using the technology to lure new business, improve efficiency and increase payouts for shareholders.
That will involve £2bn of cost cuts, which Nunn said would affect staff. “That is going to impact work. It is going to require us to continue to reskill people and hire new people, but that’s been my history for 30-odd years in financial services.”
Moody’s acknowledged the potential blow to some staff, who could be deemed replaceable as a result of new tech. Its report said there was a 20% chance that, by 2030, AI will be able to do the work of a “solid mid-level employee”.
For banks, AI might also make it easier for customers to switch to accounts offering higher interest rates, creating the possibility that large chunks of cash could be moved at short notice. “In this context, depositors’ trust in the institution and the resilience and stability of deposit funding are critical,” Moody’s said.

report.summary: Moody’s warns banks’ rapid AI adoption could create overdependence on a few Silicon Valley providers, raising outage, price, and systemic stability risks.
report.background: Financial institutions across the City and Wall Street are aggressively integrating AI to automate administrative tasks, process insurance claims, and assess creditworthiness. More than 75% of City companies now use AI, according to a UK Treasury select committee report. Moody’s acknowledges AI will eventually cut costs and boost revenues, but warns that heavy reliance on a small set of foundation model and cloud computing providers creates systemic dependency. An outage at one major provider could spread quickly across customers and sectors, while dominant vendors could eventually control pricing. This comes as generative AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic face mounting pressure to generate profits for investors, raising concerns about vendor dependence and price gouging.
key_points: Moody’s cautions that the financial sector is relying on a small set of foundation AI model and cloud providers. A single provider outage could rapidly cascade across banks and insurers, creating a systemic dependency that regulators are likely to scrutinize more closely.

While AI integration should eventually reduce costs and boost revenues in the City and on Wall Street, Moody’s says the technology requires substantial investment. Because many rivals are pursuing the same opportunities, competition will likely erode much of the expected financial benefit.

AI introduces or amplifies dangers around data privacy, cybersecurity, fraud, and deposit flight. Customers may use AI tools to switch accounts to higher-interest providers quickly, so substantial sums could move abruptly and threaten banks’ funding stability and depositor trust.

Dependence on dominant AI vendors creates price-gouging risks as OpenAI and Anthropic, among others, face pressure to turn profits. Moody’s notes that large financial firms retain proprietary data and have experience negotiating tech contracts, which may help them manage vendor dependence.

The transformation will have workforce consequences. Moody’s gives a 20% probability that by 2030 AI could perform the work of a solid mid-level employee, pushing banks like Lloyds to cut billions in costs while reskilling staff and hiring new talent.
report.impact: The financial sector is a lucrative market for AI suppliers, and any shift toward diversification could reshape competition in the industry. Banks may increasingly demand multi-cloud and multi-model strategies, open-source alternatives, and stronger governance to reduce concentration risk. Developers will need to prioritize reliability, security, explainability, and auditability to win regulated enterprise contracts. For everyday users, AI promises cheaper, faster banking and better interest rates, but it also raises risks of sudden outages, data breaches, and job displacement. Regulators may impose tighter oversight on third-party dependencies, forcing AI firms to demonstrate resilience and fair pricing. Consumers could ultimately benefit from more competition in banking, though trust and stability remain critical.
report.tools: Banks seeking to reduce vendor lock-in can explore open-source foundation models like Meta’s Llama, Mistral, and Falcon, and use orchestration frameworks such as LangChain for portable AI integration. Cloud-neutral infrastructure options including Kubernetes can also help avoid single-provider dependence. For AI risk management, watch model evaluation and governance tools like AI Fairness 360, evidently, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.
